abstract: Are technological civilizations common in our Galaxy? Ian Crawford (1997) addressed this question and concluded that extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI) or technological civilizations are not likely to be common. He brings to bear three main lines of evidence — astronomical, sociological, and biological — to reach his conclusion. Here we consider recent astronomical results and different sociological and biological lines of evidence to conclude that a Galaxy populated by tens of thousands of ETIs is still quite plausible.

articleTitle: The quest for the golden lens
abstract: Gravitational lensing is now widely and successfully used to study a range of astronomical phenomena, from individual objects like galaxies and clusters, to the mass distribution on various scales, to the overall geometry of the universe. Here we describe and assess the use of gravitational lensing as “gold standards” in addressing one of the fundamental problems in astronomy, the determination of the absolute distance scale to extragalactic objects. This is commonly parameterized by the Hubble constant, H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf>, the current expansion rate of the universe. The elegance of the underlying geometrical principle of the gravitational lensing method combined with the recent advances in observations and modelling makes it a very promising technique for measuring H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf>.

articleTitle: Predictable publicity: Proceedings of the November 1996 MIST meeting
abstract: Seismologists at the RAS/JAG Meeting on Earthquake Prediction in November last year came to the broad consensus that earthquakes are inherently unpredictable, in any precise quantitative fashion. Yet newspapers and other popular media trumpet any suggestion that quakes can be or have been predicted, without putting such claims in the context of the relevant research. But people living in areas prone to quakes want forecasts. How can these two conflicting ideas be reconciled? The answer must involve peer review and open scientific argument.

The four identical Cluster satellites were designed to orbit in close formation, measuring the charged particles, fields and waves of the near-Earth space environment. Each would have provided such high resolution data that researchers would, for the first time, have been able to discern how important structures and boundaries of the Earth's magnetosphere distort, evolve and move. The loss of this unique and exciting research capability has been a devastating blow to the worldwide community of scientists studying how particles and energy from the Sun are extracted from the solar wind and deposited in the Earth's upper atmosphere. Now there are plans to salvage as much as possible from the investment in Cluster through Cluster II. These make use of Phoenix, the one remaining Cluster satellite, which could fly around the turn of the century.

The historical record of maritime traffic over the past 400 years is a rich source of information that can be used in studies of the Earth's magnetic field. Measurements of the field were taken on board ship primarily for navigation, but they record variations in the field's morphology and intensity with time, termed the geomagnetic secular variation. This dataset is by far the most accurate source of information on the magnetic field's behaviour in the past.We are currently in the process of compiling data from the extant primary source material for the period from the 17th to the 19th century, in order to construct the most accurate representation of the magnetic field possible. Our dataset represents a tenfold increase on the number of pre-1820 observations previously used in geomagnetic studies.Although the dataset is dominated by declination, inclination and field intensity were also observed at sea as scientific interest in the geomagnetic field grew. And this temporal sequence of field measurements will become doubly valuable when compared with a snapshot of the current magnetic field from the satellite Ørsted, to be launched early next year.

articleTitle: Cool giants and supergiants: chromospheres and winds
abstract: Cool giants and supergiants reveal the presence of chromospheres and circumstellar material through emission and absorption lines over a wide range of the electromagnetic spectrum. Ultraviolet spectra, in particular, show that stellar winds and mass loss are features of cool evolved stars. Some stars have hot coronae as well as winds.Although some emission lines are formed by collisional excitation, accidental fluorescence, where strong lines of hydrogen and oxygen pump other species, plays a major role in producing the observed spectra.Possible mechanisms for heating the chromospheres of such stars include the shock dissipation of acoustic and magneto-hydrodynamic waves.

articleTitle: Comet Hale-Bopp: April fool joke or comet of the century?

abstract: The 3CR radio galaxies exhibit the same strong cosmological evolutionary effects which are found in the population of active galaxies in general. HST, VLA and UKIRT observations have been made of an almost complete sample of 28 narrow-line 3CR radio galaxies in the redshift interval 0.6< z < 1.8. The HST images show clearly the alignment effect between the optical morphologies of the galaxies and the radio axes of the double radio sources, and these can be placed in an evolutionary sequence with increasing separation of the hot-spots of the radio structures. In the case of 3C 34, there is evidence for jet-induced star formation in a galaxy which lies in the path of the radio jet. It is suggested that similar processes may play a role in creating the aligned structures. The implications of these observations for understanding the nature of the galaxies associated with strong radio sources and the K-z relationship for 3CR radio galaxies are discussed.

In August 1996 a paper was published in the journal Science announcing the apparent discovery, in a meteorite, of a primitive fossilized Martian life form (McKay et al. 1996). The implication of the observations is that there was once life on Mars. Here we outline the background to the study, the evidence presented by the NASA team, and possible alternative explanations for their observations.
